hints: Look only at the last characters of a and b. If they are equal, can they both end the trail? If not, at least one of them is useless at the end — which one?

Use a 2D DP table: dp[i][j] = longest shared trail of the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b. Each cell depends only on the cell diagonally up-left, the one above and the one to the left.

1. Make a table of size (len(a)+1) × (len(b)+1), filled with 0 (empty prefix → trail 0).
  2. For every i from 1 and every j from 1: if a[i-1] == b[j-1], set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
  3. Otherwise set dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) (drop one letter).
  4. The answer is dp[len(a)][len(b)]. Keep only two rows to save memory.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Generate every subsequence of a and check whether it is also a subsequence of b; keep the longest.

approaches.name: Memoised recursion
approaches.idea: Recurse on (i, j) with the same match / skip choices and cache results in an n×m table.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Bottom-up DP over prefixes, keeping only the previous row and the current row.

explain: Take a = "plane", b = "apple". Row by row we fill the table; whenever letters match (for example the p, l and e) the value grows by one from the diagonal, otherwise it copies the better of its top or left neighbour. The bottom-right cell ends at 3, the trail "ple". It works because the best answer for two prefixes either uses both last letters (only possible when they match) or ignores one of them. Watch for empty strings: the zero row/column already returns 0, as in "rock" vs "jazz".
recognize: Two strings + 'delete characters without reordering' + 'longest common' → a 2D DP over prefixes (the classic LCS table).
